about.title: Shafter Slip & Fall Claims
about.longDescription: Shafter is a small, tight-knit Kern County community, but that doesn't mean property owners get a pass when someone gets hurt on their premises. Whether it happened at a shop along Santa Fe Way, an apartment complex off Zerker Road, or a business near 7th Standard Road, falls often come down to a hazard that sat too long: a spill, broken pavement, poor lighting, or a loose handrail. California law asks whether the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about that danger and failed to address it. That's why documenting the scene matters so much here — photos of the hazard, witness names, and store or building surveillance footage can disappear fast if no one asks for it. LawProactive doesn't practice law itself; we simply connect injured Shafter residents with an independent attorney who can evaluate what happened, gather that evidence, and explain your options. The conversation and case review cost you nothing upfront.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Shafter Fall

items.title: Notice Has to Be Proven
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or reasonably should have known about the hazard before your fall. An attorney can help track down maintenance logs, prior complaints, or inspection records that speak to that notice.

items.title: Video Doesn't Wait Around
items.desc: Many stores and apartment complexes overwrite surveillance footage within days or weeks. An independent attorney can send a preservation request quickly so that evidence isn't lost before your claim is even reviewed.

items.title: Comparative Fault Can Reduce, Not Erase, Your Claim
items.desc: Even if you're told you were partly at fault for not seeing a hazard, California's pure comparative fault rule means you may still recover a portion of your damages. An attorney can help present your side clearly.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a slip and fall claim in Shafter?
items.answer: California generally allows two years from the date of the fall to file a premises liability lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government or public entity, the deadline is much shorter and requires an early claim to be filed. Because of that shorter window, it's worth talking to an attorney soon after the fall rather than waiting.

items.question: What if the store or landlord says the hazard was obvious?
items.answer: An obvious hazard doesn't automatically excuse a property owner from responsibility, though it can factor into comparative fault. What matters is whether the owner knew or should have known about the danger and had a reasonable chance to fix or warn about it. An independent attorney can review the specific circumstances of your fall to assess how that plays out.

items.question: I fell at a business along E Lerdo Highway — what should I do first?
items.answer: If you're able, take photos of the exact spot where you fell, note the date and time, and ask if there's surveillance video covering the area. Report the fall to management and get a written incident report if possible. Then consider having an independent attorney review your situation before evidence like video or witness memory fades.
